blurb: Colorado's own wild hollyhock: stout stems from a woody crown, big maple-like leaves, and crowded spikes of pale pink to rose-purple mallow flowers along montane streambanks and burned-over slopes. Its seeds need fire to germinate and can wait in the soil for centuries.
water: Moderate — moist, rich soil; not a xeric plant
spread: Clumping from a woody caudex; spreads only by seed, never at the root
seasons: Pink to rose-purple spikes June–August; bold maple-like foliage; dries to standing seed capsules in fall
wildlife: Showy flowers work by bees; heavily browsed by elk, mule deer, sheep and cattle
deer: Not deer resistant — elk and mule deer browse it heavily

care.hardiness: A montane native occurring east of the Cascades from British Columbia and Alberta south to Oregon and east to Colorado, where it climbs to 11,500 ft — so cold is emphatically not the limiting factor at Boulder's zone 5b–6a. In Colorado it is a mountain plant of the western and high country rather than a plains or foothills species, which is worth knowing before you site it in a hot city garden.[1][2]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, into deep, moist, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade. Pick the spot carefully — it grows from a woody caudex and resents disturbance, and it is not rhizomatous, so a damaged crown is not replaced by suckers. A large container with a moisture-retentive mix works if you keep the water up.[1][2]
care.sun: Part shade is what the Wildflower Center specifies, and that is the safer choice at our elevation and dryness; it will take full sun where the soil stays reliably moist, as it does on a wild streambank. FEIS describes it as shade-intolerant and early-seral in the wild, so deep shade is wrong too — dappled or afternoon shade is the target.[1][2]
care.soil: Moist, rich, deep, well-drained soil — FEIS describes mesic sites with deep, moist, well-drained soils. The Wildflower Center notes a low tolerance for calcium carbonate, which is a genuine caution in Boulder: very limy, high-pH clay is not its preference, so work in generous organic matter and expect it to sulk in raw alkaline subsoil.[1][2]
care.water: Moderate. It is a streambank and mountain-meadow plant that wants steady moisture, so it carries a real water cost on the semi-arid Front Range — plan on regular deep watering through summer, and don't put it in a xeric bed. It is not a bog plant either; the soil should be moist but drained.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space 2–3 ft apart. It is a substantial plant — commonly 1.5–3 ft in drier spots and up to 6 ft where it is happy — with big bold leaves, so give it room.[1][2]
care.propagation: By seed only; it reproduces by seed and is not rhizomatous, so division is not an option. The seed is the interesting part: it has a smooth, hard coat and requires heat treatment to germinate, which is why the species erupts after wildfire. For garden sowing that means mechanical scarification or a brief hot-water treatment — untreated seed will simply sit. Propagation protocols are published through the Native Plants Network.[2][1]
care.sow: Scarify or heat-treat the seed, then sow in fall or start indoors in spring; keep the medium moist. Seed remains viable in soil for at least a few hundred years — up to 91% still viable in buried seed banks — so old collected seed is worth trying.[2]
care.bloom: June through August, in showy pink, rose-purple or nearly white mallow flowers crowded into dense clusters on stout stalks. In Colorado the display comes at high summer, and it is the closest thing our native flora has to a garden hollyhock.[1][2]
care.maintenance: Low once established. Cut the dried stalks down in late winter, or leave them standing for the seed capsules. Mulch to hold soil moisture. If you garden where elk or deer visit, fence it — this is one of the most heavily browsed plants in its range, not a deer-resistant native.[2][1]
care.troubles: Few diseases. The two real problems are cultural and biological: drought stress in a dry, sunny site, and browsing. FEIS records it as highly preferred by sheep and cattle in recently burned aspen stands and heavily used by elk and mule deer in burned areas of Grand Teton and Yellowstone — with crude protein up to 22%, it is genuinely good forage, so expect wildlife to find it.[2]

edible.summary: No documented human food use; it is excellent wildlife and livestock forage, which is not the same thing.[1][2]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a human food use for streambank wild hollyhock, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. Note carefully that its high forage value for elk, deer, sheep and cattle (crude protein 12–22%) says nothing about human edibility, and neither FEIS nor the Wildflower Center records any toxicity. Do not reason across from the edible mallows in this guide. If you meet it in the mountains, leave it alone: it is a native plant of montane streambanks and post-fire slopes, and in a burned area it is doing the work of holding the soil together.[1][2]
